title: Dates and times
summary: Work with dates and times in lubridate. Parse and build them, round to weeks, explore clock changes, and move between time zones.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes lubridate

steps.explain: `library(tidyverse)` attaches lubridate, whose functions parse, take apart and do arithmetic with dates and times.

steps.title: Parse dates and times

runs.purpose: turn text into a date-time in Larkhaven's time zone
runs.task: Parse "2025-03-09 01:41:07" with `ymd_hms()`, in the time zone "America/Toronto".

runs.purpose: parse a date written the American way, month first

alternatives: trips = read_csv('data/trips.csv', locale = locale(tz = 'America/Toronto'), show_col_types = FALSE)
runs.purpose: read every 2025 trip, with its times in Larkhaven's time zone, into `trips`

steps.explain:
lubridate's parsers are named for the order of a date's parts: `ymd_hms()` for year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds, and `mdy()` for the American month-first dates in the station exports.

A date-time is an instant, and its clock time depends on where you are, so `tz` says where: Larkhaven keeps the same time as Toronto, EST in winter and EDT in summer. The trip file records clock times without a time zone, and `read_csv()` would read them as UTC; its `locale` gives them Larkhaven's.

steps.title: Take apart and build: wday(), make_date()

alternatives: trips |> mutate(day = wday(started_at, label = TRUE)) |> count(day)

values.top_day: local({c <- count(trips, day = wday(started_at, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)); as.character(c$day[which.max(c$n)])})

runs.purpose: count the trips on each day of the week
runs.task: Count the trips by `day`, the day of the week of `started_at` with `wday(label = TRUE)`.

runs.purpose: make the first day of each month of 2025 from its parts
runs.task: Make the first day of each month of 2025 with `make_date()`: year 2025, months `1:12`, day 1.

steps.explain:
`year()`, `month()`, `day()`, `hour()`, `minute()` and `wday()` each take one part out of a date-time; `label = TRUE` names the day or month as an ordered factor, so the days count from Sunday to Saturday. The days of the week are nearly level, {top_day} just ahead.

`make_date()` and `make_datetime()` go the other way, building dates from parts held in separate numbers, and work on vectors: `1:12` gives a date for every month.

steps.title: Round to weeks: floor_date()

runs.code:
trips |>
  count(week = floor_date(started_at, "week", week_start = 1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = n)) +
  geom_line()
alternatives: trips |> mutate(week = floor_date(started_at, unit = 'week', week_start = 1)) |> count(week) |> ggplot(aes(week, n)) + geom_line()
runs.purpose: count the trips in each week, each week starting on a Monday, and draw the counts as a line
runs.task: Count trips by `week`. Round `started_at` down to Monday with `floor_date(started_at, "week", week_start = 1)`. Draw `n` against `week` as a line.

steps.explain:
`floor_date()` rounds a date-time down to the start of a unit, here the Monday the trip's week began, so all of a week's trips count together: {n_weeks} weeks, as the first and last are partial weeks. The busiest week began on {top_week}. `round_date()` and `ceiling_date()` round to the nearest or up.

Rounding to a week smooths out the weekday-weekend wobble in the daily counts, so the seasons show.

steps.title: When the clocks change: durations and periods

runs.purpose: keep the trip that crossed the change to summer time, as `spring`
runs.task: Keep the trip whose `trip_id` is 370330 and store it in `spring`.

runs.purpose: work out how long that trip took
add one day to its start, first as 24 hours and then as a calendar day
runs.task: Add a day to `spring$started_at` twice, in one vector: as a duration, `ddays(1)`, and as a period, `days(1)`.

steps.explain:
Trip 370330 started at 1:41 on 9 March and ended at 3:07, {clock_gap} minutes later by the clock. But at 2:00 that night the clocks jumped to 3:00, so the trip really took {recorded} minutes, which is what subtracting date-times in the right time zone gives.

A duration, such as `ddays(1)`, is an exact number of seconds: 24 hours after 1:41 on 9 March, a day only 23 hours long, is 2:41 the next day. A period, such as `days(1)`, follows the calendar: the same clock time the next day, 1:41.

Use periods for "the same time tomorrow" and durations for elapsed time.

steps.title: Time zones: with_tz() and force_tz()

runs.purpose: show the same instant on a UTC clock
keep the clock time but say it is UTC, which makes it a different instant
runs.task: Keep the clock time of `spring$started_at` but set its time zone to UTC with `force_tz()`.

runs.purpose: find trips that ended before they started by the clock, though they took some time
runs.task: Keep the trips whose `ended_at` is before `started_at`, but whose `duration_min` is above 0.

steps.explain:
`with_tz()` changes the clock a time is shown on, not the instant: 1:41 in Larkhaven is 6:41 in UTC. `force_tz()` keeps the clock time and changes the time zone, so it moves the instant: use it to correct a time read in the wrong zone.

The {n_backwards} trips the filter finds started in the first 1 am on 2 November and ended in the second, after the clocks went back an hour. Clock times can't tell the two 1 ams apart, so these trips seem to end before they start; their `duration_min`, recorded by the scheme, is right.

steps.title: Today: today()
steps.explain: `today()` gives the date where R is running, and `now()` the date-time; both change every time you run them, so the coach checks only their shape. Dates are stored as the number of days since 1 January 1970, which is why subtracting two of them gives a number of days.
